summaryBox.title: Quick Section Summary
summaryBox.takeaway: Interstitial fluid filtered from capillaries enters lymphatic capillaries to form Lymph. Lymph lacks RBCs/platelets, has lower proteins, and high lymphocytes. Intestinal Lacteals absorb fat as Chyle.

conceptBreakdown.codeSnippet:
INTERSTITIAL FLUID vs LYMPH
                         
   Capillary Hydrostatic Pressure ──► Fluid filtered out ──► Interstitial Fluid (Tissue Fluid)
                                                                    │
   Drained into Lymphatic Capillaries ◄─────────────────────────────┘
                                   │
   Transformed into LYMPH ──► Returned to Systemic Veins (Subclavian Veins)
conceptBreakdown.content:
As blood flows under hydrostatic pressure through tissue capillaries, water and small water-soluble solutes pass through capillary pores into intercellular spaces, forming **Interstitial Fluid (Tissue Fluid)**.

* **Composition of Lymph**: A colorless fluid identical in electrolyte concentration to plasma, but containing **fewer plasma proteins**, **no RBCs or platelets**, and **high concentrations of Lymphocytes**.
* **Specialized Lacteals**: Lymphatic capillaries located in intestinal villi (**Lacteals**) absorb and transport digested dietary fats (**Chyle**) as emulsified chylomicrons into the systemic venous circulation via the **Thoracic Duct**.
